extraction.research_question: Are campaign donations and lobbying activity linked for the same interest group-politician pair, and do donations precede lobbying on bills tied to the donee's committee seats, sponsorship or co-sponsorship (the "access-buying" hypothesis)?
extraction.theory: Two camps on campaign money: donations as ideology or electoral competition (Poole and Romer 1985; Poole, Romer and Rosenthal 1987) versus donations as long-term strategic investments for access (Langbein 1986; Austen-Smith 1995; Esterling 2007; Richter and Werner 2017; Barber, Canes-Wrone and Thrower 2017). Lobbying either conveys information (Austen-Smith and Wright 1992; Potters and Van Winden 1992) or serves as a legislative subsidy to allies (Hall and Deardorff 2006). The paper tests the access-buying direction (donation precedes lobbying) and sets aside rewards (fn 9).
extraction.data: Unit: firm-politician-year dyad. Sample: all publicly traded U.S. manufacturing firms (NAICS 31-33; 2,703 firms that lobbied or donated at least once) and all 979 members of the House and Senate serving 2008-2018 (text uses 2008-2017 in places). Result: an unbalanced panel of 2,646,237 unique firm-politician dyads and 16,428,834 observations. Sources: Lobbying Disclosure Act reports (over 1.2 million parsed; over 75 million reports plus FEC filings combined since 1999 per abstract; lobbying data from 1999, bill-level quality from 2008 after the HLOGA amendment); FEC itemized contributions (about 53 million individual contributions, four million employer names, 827,000 occupation names, 1980-2018); Compustat gvkey; SOC codes; GovTrack IDs; Volden and Wiseman (2018) politician covariates; Groseclose and Stewart (1998) committee scores. Broader descriptive coverage: over 84,000 interest groups (abstract, p. 2). Descriptive 2013 snapshot: 11,829 public companies and 553 members of Congress (6,541,437 possible dyads). Appendix E: 1999/2000 interest-group comparison.
extraction.method: Step 1: descriptive tables and cross-sectional log-log fits (Table 2, Fig 2, Appendix C and E). Step 2: linear probability models with firm, year, politician and firm-politician fixed effects, with controls for party, majority status, committee chair and powerful-committee membership (Table 3, Table F.1; standard errors clustered by firm). Step 3: difference-in-differences combined with matching (Imai, Kim and Wang 2020). Treated pairs are first-time donors defined over L = 3 years. Matched controls are other firms with no donation to the same politician in t to t-3. Matching uses Mahalanobis distance on sales, employees and pre-treatment lobbying, with 10 closest comparators. The DiD estimator (Eq. 4) differences outcome changes between t-1 and t+F for treated pairs versus the matched mean, averaged over pairs. Confidence intervals come from a block bootstrap. Outcome: Y=1 if the firm lobbies a bill that is sponsored, co-sponsored, or assigned to a committee on which the politician serves (each measured separately).
extraction.scope: Population: publicly traded U.S. manufacturing firms and House and Senate members, 2008-2017/2018 (main analysis). Institution: U.S. Congress and federal lobbying disclosure. Era: LDA electronic filing era (1999 on; bill-level data from 2008). Excludes private firms, trade and industry associations, ideological groups, unions and nonprofits from the main analysis. Congress is the relevant lobbied institution; agencies are about 3.4% of reports (p. 5).

key_findings.finding: Descriptive 2013 snapshot: only 519 of 11,829 public companies (about 4%) both donated and lobbied, yet they account for most money in politics.
Firm-politician dyads with both donations and bill-related lobbying are extremely rare but carry large money: 13,886 dyads out of 6,541,437 possible.
key_findings.location: Sec 2.1, printed p. 13 (PDF p. 15), Table 2 right panel
key_findings.numbers: 13,886 dyads (<0.1% of all possible); more than $520 million, 17% of 2013 spending; 15,420 donation-only dyads, 13,078 of them from employee donations

key_findings.finding: Firm-level corporate PAC donations and lobbying spending are positively related for firms doing both.
key_findings.numbers: Log-log slope beta = 0.88, adjusted R2 about 0.4; text says a 10% PAC increase goes with 8.8% more lobbying, while the Fig 2 caption computes 8.7%

key_findings.finding: Other donation types show the same firm-level pattern (all donations, executives, employees, government relations).
key_findings.numbers: beta 0.58 (R2 0.29) all donations; 0.58 (0.17) executives; 0.68 (0.23) employees; 0.78 (0.20) government relations; years 2000-2017

key_findings.finding: Within firm-politician pairs, a firm's first-time donation raises the probability it lobbies a bill tied to that politician in the same year.
key_findings.numbers: Donation coefficient 0.102-0.118 (SEs about 0.008-0.009), N = 16,428,834. Firm-politician and year FE (last column) gives 0.118. Baseline probability about 0.05; sponsors 0.002, co-sponsors 0.026, committee members 0.043

key_findings.finding: Donation amount matters at the margin: a 10% larger first-time donation goes with about 0.15 percentage points higher probability of lobbying a related bill.
key_findings.numbers: Donation Amount coefficient 0.015-0.017 per log unit (SE 0.001); about 0.15 pp per 10%

key_findings.finding: Under difference-in-differences with matching, a donation raises the probability the pair lobbies related bills by about 8.5 points in the donation year, falling to about 3 points by three years later.
key_findings.location: Sec 3.2, Fig 5 (printed p. 20-21); caption gives 8.5 falling to 3.2 pp
key_findings.numbers: Senate t+0 about 0.085, t+3 about 0.03; House effects larger (no number given in text); effects disappear within two to three years

key_findings.finding: Effects are concentrated in committee-related lobbying. Corporate PAC donations show the largest effects, but CEO and employee donations are also positive. The same-firm sponsor link is positive but short-lived.
key_findings.numbers: Qualitative: committee effects largest; PAC > CEO and employee; no numeric values in text

key_findings.finding: Robustness to firm-level covariates (sales, employees) leaves the donation coefficient essentially unchanged.
key_findings.numbers: Donation coefficient 0.104-0.123 across eight models; N = 7,189,477 for covariate-controlled models; adjusted R2 0.450-0.544

key_findings.finding: The Ansolabehere, Snyder and Tripathi (2002) pattern holds for the 1999/2000 interest-group data, with the strongest PAC-lobbying relation for corporations.
key_findings.location: Appendix E, Fig E.1 (appendix p. 6); cube-root scale
key_findings.numbers: beta: corporations 2.0; membership organizations 1.6; trade associations 0.8; labor unions 0.6 (described as not present)

key_findings.finding: Illustrative cases: Farenthold (Exxon Mobil PAC) and Lockheed Martin-Bill Nelson show donations followed by related bills and sponsorship.
key_findings.numbers: Farenthold received $3,000 from Exxon's PAC in his first year; Nelson received $9,000 from Lockheed's PAC in 2011 and $22,000 from executives and employees in 2012

limitations: Main analysis covers only publicly traded U.S. manufacturing firms; private firms, trade associations, ideological groups and unions are excluded (printed p. 24).
Donations through industry associations, ideological groups and nonprofits are not captured; the authors say this may understate donation effects on access (printed p. 24).

Lobbying-to-politician links rely on bills named in LDA reports. Per-bill lobbying dollars are allocated evenly across connected politicians, which the authors call a highly noisy measure (printed p. 8). Bill success is not modeled (printed p. 24).
Access-buying is inferred from timing, not from measured private connections; the reverse (rewards) direction is explicitly left for future work (fn 9, printed p. 14-15).
Name disambiguation is heuristic with hand validation; a graph neural network upgrade is noted as in progress (fn 6, printed p. 6).

Sample period is stated inconsistently: abstract and Sec 2 say 2000 or 1999 onward, p. 2 says 2000-2018, p. 12 says 2008-2018, and the main estimates use 2008-2017. Donation-to-lobbying elasticity is 8.8% in text versus 8.7% in the Fig 2 caption. Fig C.1 caption says cubed USD while the axes are logged.

Effects are estimated relative to a low base rate (about 0.05), so 8.5 points is large in relative terms but small in levels. The linear probability models rely on parametric assumptions, as the paper acknowledges (printed p. 17). The DiD estimator is conservative and underpowered per Imai, Kim and Wang (2020), per fn 18.
Estimates are associations within matched designs, not proof of quid pro quo; the paper itself disclaims causal reading of the reverse direction.
Journal publication is not in the PDF; the 2026 Journal of Politics listing is taken from the metadata hint only.

summary_md:
Kim, Stuckatz and Wolters link LDA bill mentions to FEC donations for U.S. public manufacturing firms (2,703 firms, 979 members of Congress, 2008-2017, 16.4M firm-politician-year rows). They test whether a donation comes before lobbying on bills that the recipient sponsored, cosponsored or handled in committee. In the descriptive 2013 snapshot, only 519 of 11,829 public firms both donated and lobbied, and they account for about 85% of the money. Under firm-politician fixed effects, a first-time donation (no gift in the prior 3 years) goes with a 10-12 point higher chance of lobbying a related bill in the same year, against a base rate of about 0.05. Matched difference-in-differences gives about 8.5 points at year t (Senate), falling to about 3 points by t+3. The effect is concentrated in committee-related lobbying and is largest for corporate PACs. The authors read this as access-buying timing, not quid pro quo.

For Paul's systems, the paper matters mainly because its estimand differs from what the system measured. The FEC-to-LDA bridge (round 3) is a cross-sectional member-by-industry-by-cycle rank correlation. It is dominated by trade associations, credits only sponsors and cosponsors, and controls for finance-committee seats. Its four-control partial of about 0 does not contradict a within-pair, onset-timed, committee-driven effect among public firms. The bridge design actually controls away the channel Kim finds strongest. The paper also cuts against the system's "FEC leads LDA by 42 months" heuristic: its effect is concurrent and gone within two to three years.

The paper also builds its outcome from the same bill-roster join that the system ruled circular. It escapes circularity only because its treatment, the donation, is timed independently of the join. Its identity work (gvkey matching, constrained graph clustering, hand-coded validation) is a method source for Mentat's donor ladder. Every figure here is the paper's own; none has been reproduced locally (UNVERIFIED per DE-062).

Annotation document a0d42782bc20 (source text: C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\_text\a0d42782bc20.txt, read in full, 9 cited works). No annotation JSON exists at C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\_annots\a0d42782bc20.json, so there are no reviewer comments or highlights to add. Paul's annotations are the only commentary. Where he says "the present research" or "the current research" without naming a system, the system links below are inferred from the task framing (Melange path-finding, SNA and allocation; Moneyball scoring; Mentat; Terrier) and are marked as such in the takeaways.

Overarching argument: Paul's reading treats the literature as a stack that feeds his systems in order: (1) measuring traits or positions from text, (2) turning text and filings into network nodes and edges, (3) finding paths and communities in that graph, (4) using influence and lobbying-return evidence to set allocation and fundraising targets. He consistently rates the works by how directly they supply a pre-built pipeline or a method he can reuse.

Research questions Paul raises: how to convert an individual's text-derived trait score into a social-network node (Birkenmaier); how to disentangle ambiguous statements; how to turn a bipartite lobbying model into a graph that path-finding can run on (Kim and Kunisky); how to treat negative sentiment in influence edges and how to score agreement between actors when sentiment is negative (Fink); whether reply and mention edges are negative; how to add temporal weighting so shifting relationships are captured (Fink, Malaterre); how to separate campaign donations from events and meetings in return models (Huneeus and Kim); whether the allocation model should differentiate representatives by state-layer industry presence (Huneeus and Kim); whether ideologically aligned think-tank funding should enter allocation models (Furnas et al.).

Syntheses across works: Louvain community detection recurs in Ardekani et al. and Malaterre and Lareau, and Paul applies it to communities and coalitions. Two works share the author In Song Kim (Huneeus and Kim; Kim and Kunisky), and Paul's notes on them connect lobbying returns to network structure. Kim et al. Overarching arguments: (1) The existing structural join (build_dyad_bill_sets, every sponsor and cosponsor of every bill an org cites) answers "whose bills did this org lobby on," not "whom did this org plausibly contact." Scope note: 187fc1d3356c.txt is not a literature annotation document. It is the DRAFT prereg/evaluation plan ("Contact Inference Layer - Effectiveness Evaluation Plan", dated 2026-08-27, revised 2026-08-28) for the contact-inference layer, which is a companion to CONTACT_INFERENCE_DESIGN.md. It has no reviewer comments or highlights, and no _annots/187fc1d3356c.json exists (checked the 63-file _annots folder). The only external works it cites are the LobbyView family, so entries below cover those and nothing else. The doc contains no annotated bibliography, so the per-work takeaways are close paraphrases of how the plan uses or discounts LobbyView, not Paul's commentary on a reading list.

Overarching argument: the layer's claim is a ranking-and-calibration claim, not a causal one. Fused contact-plausibility scores should rank disclosed lobbying targets above matched non-targets better than the deployed n_bills ordering (B1, +0.10 AUC margin) and an employment-only LobbyView-style prior (B2, Platt-calibrated, +0.05 margin), at calibration good enough to publish as an annotation. Nothing in the evaluation can establish that any inferred contact occurred.

Research questions and design: (1) whether fusion beats B1 and B2 on a held-out, org-grouped half; (2) whether calibration (Brier skill score vs prevalence, reliability bins) is sound; (3) what share of the eligible blast radius gets scored (coverage), with outcomes PASS / COVERAGE / MISS / RETIRED. The discipline is prereg, then power check, then battery of negative controls, then ONE look.

Syntheses and gates: the 4,549-activity honorific-name pool is a full-corpus upper bound, but the layer scores only a 770-org financial scope. Measured in-scope intersection is about 36 hits across 6 orgs (strict) or 248 (ceiling), versus bars of at least 600 rows and 40 orgs, so an in-scope-only run is near-certainly a power NO-GO. Gate E1 (Paul's ruling pending) chooses among E1-a (in-scope only, expected NO-GO), E1-b (corpus-wide validation plus one declared transport assumption, the working assumption), or E1-c (defer). Gate G3 (adjudication ownership, press-classification precedent) and G6 are also Paul's.

Stated gaps and caveats: (a) disclosure-culture confound: orgs that name targets may differ from silent orgs, so transport is an assumption; (b) negatives may be contaminated by pattern false negatives, bounded by a 100-description recall check; (c) there is no external accuracy benchmark for contact inference (the LobbyView papers report none); (d) the org-level clustered SE may exceed the B2 margin, in which case the result is inconclusive-by-power, not PASS; (e) LDA does not require disclosure of contacts, so scores are inferences, never records of meetings. Barred wording includes "lobbied member" and "contacted member" for inferred rows.

Look ledger: the 2026-08-28 adversarial review is the only completed entry. E1 ruling, pilot power check, adjudication freeze, battery, abstention floor, and THE look are all unfilled. No look has been taken.

summary_issues: 'A first-time donation (no gift in the prior 3 years)' is attached to the FE estimates; Table 3's text sets L = t-1, and the 3-year (L=3) window is the DiD's definition.

'Its effect is concurrent and gone within two to three years' sits beside 'falling to about 3 points by t+3'; Fig 5 still shows about 3.2 pp at t+3. The 2-3 year disappearance is the authors' gloss on Fig 6.

The claim that the paper 'cuts against the system's FEC leads LDA by 42 months heuristic' is a category error: in the brain (lobbyview-collector.md:124) and memory, 42 months is the FEC-vs-LobbyView data freshness gap, not a measured behavioral lag.

'The bridge design actually controls away the channel Kim finds strongest' overstates: Kim's committee channel is part of the outcome definition (lobbying bills referred to the member's committee), and Kim also controls for powerful-committee membership; the bridge's real gap is that its Y lacks the committee-referral channel.

'Matched difference-in-differences gives about 8.5 points' is the Senate figure; the abstract presents 8.5 pp without the chamber split and the House is only described as 'even stronger'. Quote as Senate, year t, or label UNSTRATIFIED.

Related link imai-2021-fixed-effects-regression removed: this paper does not cite Imai and Kim (2021); it cites Imai, Kim and Wang (2020) for matched TSCS DiD, so 'Imai and Kim's critique motivates the switch' is unsupported.
Bonica link: the paper cites Bonica 2017 (DIME) for name standardization, not 'Bonica's DIME donor data', and cites Bonica 2014 (the related item) only for the ideology-score caveat.
gaps_exposed: The bridge's Y (rebuilt LDA attention) credits only sponsor and cosponsor rosters. The committee-referral channel, which carries Kim's largest effect, is absent from the join even though build_network_2021_rebuild.py parses committee_referrals. The committee control then absorbs whatever committee-driven signal is left.

There is no within-pair, onset-timed design anywhere in the system. Every FEC-LDA test is cross-sectional and concurrent, so Kim's estimand (first-time donation, then lobbying in the same year, matched DiD) has never been tested locally.

The system has no measure of how long an access effect lasts. Money enters the flip model and C3 as cycle-level levels; Kim shows the effect fades within 2-3 years and is concentrated at donation onset.

There is no firm-level (corporate) identity layer in the lobbying lane. Clients are mostly associations, which Kim excludes and finds weaker for (trade-association slope 0.8 vs corporations 2.0, Appendix E).
Mentat's identity ladder has no measured precision or recall. Kim's hand-coded cross-validation is the missing step.
flags: D-021: Kim builds firm-politician edges and weights (Fig 1; per-bill lobbying $ allocated across connected politicians) from LDA bill mentions. Adopting that construction would make LDA an edge and weight source. Use LDA only for identity; any edge would have to come from the donation side or another source.

extraction.research_question: Can the linear two-way fixed effects (2FE) regression with unit and time fixed effects be justified as a design-based, nonparametric causal estimator for panel data, both (a) as an adjustment for unit-specific and time-specific unobserved confounders at once and (b) as equivalent to the difference-in-differences (DiD) estimator beyond the two-group, two-period case?
extraction.theory: Matching representation of fixed effects estimators (extending Imai and Kim 2019 from unit FE to two-way FE) and the parallel trends assumption of the multi-period DiD design (Assumption 1, PDF p.7). The paper's goal is to clarify two common misunderstandings of 2FE, not to propose a new estimator (PDF p.3).
extraction.data: None. This is an analytical paper with no empirical dataset, sample, time period or reported N. Setting: a panel of N units i=1..N and T periods t=1..T, binary treatment X_it, outcome Y_it, balanced for notational simplicity (unbalanced extension asserted as straightforward, PDF p.3). The only numbers are an illustrative treatment matrix with N=5 units and T=4 periods (Figure 1, PDF pp.4-5).
extraction.method: Algebraic/proof-based analysis. Proposition 1 (PDF p.4): the 2FE estimator (eq. 2) equals a two-way matching estimator with adjustment factor K. Proposition 2 (PDF p.6): a matching estimator using only opposite-status matches equals a weighted 2FE estimator with weights K_it. Section 4: multi-period DiD (eq. 12, PDF p.8) defined via matched sets (eqs. 9-11, PDF p.8) and shown to equal a weighted 2FE estimator with weights W_it (Theorem 1, PDF p.9; proof Appendix A, PDF p.10). Proofs of Propositions 1-2 are in the Online Supplementary Information. No simulation or empirical application appears in the text.
extraction.identification: No new identification strategy is proposed. The paper states that under the multi-period DiD design with parallel trends (Assumption 1, PDF p.7), the estimand is the ATT, tau = E(Y_it(1) - Y_it(0) | X_it=1, X_i,t-1=0) (eq. 8, PDF p.7). Footnote 2 (PDF p.9): if model (1) is correct, the 2FE estimator is consistent for tau under the multi-period DiD design (beta = tau). The paper argues that this validity rests on the linear model, not on design.
extraction.scope: General panel data with a binary treatment in which units can switch into and out of treatment at different times (not only staggered adoption, PDF p.3). No population, institution or era is studied; the paper is methodological and makes no claims about a particular substantive field.

key_findings.finding: The 2FE estimator can be written as a two-way matching estimator in which each counterfactual is built from the same-unit average, same-time average, minus a pooled adjustment-set average, with a factor K equal to the net proportion of proper (opposite-status) matches.
key_findings.numbers: Adjustment set size |A_it| = |M_it| x |N_it| (eq. 4, PDF p.4)

key_findings.finding: Simultaneous nonparametric adjustment for unit-specific and time-specific confounders is impossible under 2FE: mismatches (same-status observations) and an adjustment set containing observations sharing neither the unit nor the time period remain even after restricting to opposite-status matches (Proposition 2).
key_findings.location: Section 3.2, PDF pp.5-6; Figure 1 caption PDF p.5
key_findings.numbers: Illustrative example: a_it = 2 mismatches in adjustment set of size 4, so K_it = 1 + 2/4 = 3/2 (PDF p.6)

key_findings.finding: Under the multi-period DiD design, all three sets (within-unit matched, within-time matched, adjustment) contain only control observations, so mismatches are eliminated.
key_findings.location: Section 4, Figure 2 and eqs. 9-11, PDF p.8

key_findings.finding: The multi-period DiD estimator equals a weighted 2FE estimator; the unweighted 2FE estimator is not in general equivalent to it, contrary to common belief.
key_findings.location: Theorem 1 and text after it, PDF p.9

key_findings.finding: Some control observations receive negative regression weights, which occurs when (2X_it - 1)(2X_i't' - 1) = -1, i.e., when a control enters the adjustment set for multiple treated observations.
key_findings.location: Theorem 1 weights and discussion, PDF p.9
key_findings.numbers: Weight product equal to -1 (no empirical magnitude reported)

key_findings.finding: The DiD-2FE equivalence holds only in the simplest two-group, two-period setting; with more periods and units switching in and out, the justification of 2FE as DiD requires the linearity assumption.
key_findings.location: Section 4.2 opening and discussion, PDF pp.8-9
key_findings.numbers: Two periods, two groups (no numbers)

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: 2FE is not a design-based, nonparametric causal estimator; its validity fundamentally rests on modeling assumptions. Future work should develop design-based panel estimators (e.g., synthetic control extensions).
key_findings.location: Abstract PDF p.2; Section 5 PDF p.10

summary_md:
Imai and Kim (Political Analysis 29(3), 2021) ask whether the standard linear two-way fixed effects regression (unit plus time dummies) can be read as a design-based, nonparametric causal estimator. Their answer is no. Proposition 1 (PDF p.4) rewrites the 2FE estimator as a matching estimator that builds each counterfactual from three averages: the same unit, the same period, and an adjustment set of size |M_it| x |N_it|. Because that adjustment set includes observations with the same treatment status ("mismatches"), the estimator cannot adjust nonparametrically for unit and time confounders at the same time. Mismatches tend to cause attenuation bias. In the toy example, 2 mismatches in an adjustment set of 4 give K = 3/2 (PDF pp.5-6). The multi-period difference-in-differences estimator, where treatment can switch on and off, equals a weighted 2FE estimator in which some control observations get negative weights (Theorem 1, PDF p.9). The unweighted 2FE estimator equals DiD only in the 2-group, 2-period case. So the causal reading of 2FE depends on the linear additive model, not on the design. The paper is purely analytical: no data, no simulation, binary treatment only. Its software is the R package wfe.

For Paul's systems, this paper bears on one place: the Mentat sector-growth study. That study fits sector-baseline OLS and treats sector+year FE, log-FE and first-difference-with-year-effects variants as robustness checks. On the L-LV lobbying tests the growth slope flips sign under year FE (L3-LV +0.352 to -0.477). The paper explains why this is expected. One-way and two-way FE weight sector-years differently, and the 2FE coefficient is a model-dependent weighted contrast, not a DiD estimate. Sign agreement across those variants is therefore not agreement on a single causal estimand. The DECEL dummy, which switches on and off within each sector, is the paper's exact setting. No other component estimates a causal effect from a panel with unit and time fixed effects.

'The unweighted 2FE estimator equals DiD only in the 2-group, 2-period case' is stronger than the text: the paper says unweighted 2FE is not in general equivalent to multi-period DiD and cites the 2x2 case as the common justification.
gaps_exposed: The sector-growth study has no signed per-observation weight diagnostic for its FE regressions. Temporal support reports only absolute weight shares by year (sgs_review.R:252-257), so it cannot show negative-weight sector-years, which Theorem 1 says arise with switching binary treatments such as DECEL.

The study has no design-based panel comparison (matched multi-period DiD via wfe/PanelMatch, or synthetic-control-style estimators) for the binary DECEL/ASYM terms. Every variant in the robustness family (base, R-yearFE, R-logFE, R-FD, FDY) is a linear additive model, so they share the same modelling assumption the paper identifies.

No parallel-trends check (pre-period placebo or event-study leads) is recorded for any sector-FE growth or DECEL test. The paper names parallel trends (Assumption 1) as the identifying condition for the DiD reading.
flags: Paul's 'trend over significance' directive (2026-09-26) treats sign consistency across variants as evidence. The paper implies that the one-way FE, two-way FE and first-difference variants target differently weighted contrasts, so a sign flip between them (L3-LV +0.352 vs -0.477) means different estimands rather than noise. Sign agreement across those specs should not be cited as a consistent trend in one causal effect.

Year-effect variants are reported without strata (sgs_estimate.R:398 sets no_strata for year-effect fits other than the year_fe variant). Under the brain wording rule, any pooled FE coefficient quoted across the sector fault line must carry strata or the UNSTRATIFIED label.
No conflict with the rejected SNA proposals, D-021, D-025 or D-104..D-108. The paper does not address networks, LDA edges or reciprocity.
paul_alignment: Paul's highlights focus on the paper's central claims: 2FE 'critically relies upon the assumption of linear additive effects', its validity 'fundamentally rests on the modeling assumptions', and DiD equals weighted 2FE with negative weights. His positions table cites this paper for the sector-growth study ('Imai & Kim's 2FE caution bears on the design') and for single-look discipline. That reading matches the evidence. The sector-growth lane learned the same lesson the hard way: L3-LV was called 'supported' before the year-FE check, then flipped sign. His annotation record for this paper is empty (no takeaways, no system links), so his note is not stale; it simply was never written. One tension: his 'trend over significance' directive accepts sign stability as the bar, while this paper implies that sign stability across one-way FE, two-way FE and first-difference specs is not stability of one causal quantity. For single-look discipline the paper bears only indirectly: a pre-registered look on a 2FE spec tests a linear model, not a design. Nothing sharper holds there, so no bearing was assigned.

Blackwell and Yamauchi's IPTW with unit fixed effects in the propensity model for marginal structural models (citing Imai and Kim 2019 on linear FE limits) is a weighting-based alternative of the kind Imai and Kim's conclusion calls for (PDF p.10).

extraction.research_question: Do electoral incentives change how legislators allocate effort to visible activities (bill sponsorship, committee service, floor attendance), and do they change ideological positioning? The paper uses term limits as the source of variation in incentives.
extraction.theory: Electoral accountability models (Alt, Bueno de Mesquita and Rose 2011, reviewed in the Appendix): voters cannot observe competence directly and infer it from observable effort, so reelection-minded incumbents should allocate more effort to visible activities. Removing reelection incentives (term-limited final term) should reduce that effort. For ideology, the paper contrasts the marginality hypothesis (Fiorina 1973; Downs-style moderation), ideological shirking (Bender and Lott 1996), pandering (Canes-Wrone, Herron and Shotts 2001) and citizen-candidate models (fixed positions). Null ideological effects are read as consistent with citizen-candidate models and with voter inattention to platforms (p.671-674).
extraction.data: Sample: legislator-term panel from 14 U.S. states whose legislatures have term limits of three or more terms (16 chambers: 14 houses plus the AZ and ME senates; Table 1, p.665). Nebraska (unicameral) and staggered-term senates are excluded. Coverage ranges by state (e.g., AZ 1991-2016, OH 2007-2014; Table 1). Outcome samples (Tables 2-4): roll-call attendance N=11,109 legislator-terms, 4,642 legislators; bills N=16,727, 6,207 legislators; committee activity N=16,255, 6,123 legislators (Table 4). Additional controls for Table 3 col 4: New York and Texas (non-term-limited), matched synthetic controls, N=11,416, 1,506 legislators. Scale: about 780,000 bills, over 16 million roll-call votes linked to candidates, about 6,200 legislators, and over 80,000 interest-group ratings (intro and abstract, p.662-663). Data were hand-collected from official state sources, about 100 hours per state (p.665). Election returns from Klarner et al. (2013), cleaned in Fouirnaies and Hall (2018).
extraction.method: OLS difference-in-differences at the individual level (eq. 3, p.669): Productivity_ict = beta * TermLimited_ict + alpha_i + delta_ct + eps_ict, with legislator fixed effects and chamber-year (or chamber-party-year) fixed effects; robust SEs clustered by legislator. Outcome is a PCA-based productivity index (first principal component of log bills sponsored, a committee activity index, and percent of floor votes cast; normalized mean 0, SD 1; p.667). Committee index weights: 0 non-member, 1 member, 2 vice chair, 3 chair, summed across committees (eq. 1-2, p.666). Ideology: W-NOMINATE first dimension, absolute value as extremity, and party-split W-NOMINATE (Table 5, p.673). Interest-group ratings (0-100) across abortion, business, education, environment, guns, taxes, labor unions and an "other" category, estimated with legislator-by-group and group-by-chamber-year fixed effects (eq. 4, p.672). Robustness: log seniority, seniority FE, cohort-year FE, and matched NY/TX synthetic controls with match-pair-year FE (Table 3, p.670).
extraction.identification: Within-person comparison: each incumbent's change in effort on entering the binding final term is compared with contemporaneous legislators in the same chamber-year who are not yet termed out, which holds fixed time-invariant individual type (Alt et al. selection problem, p.664-665). The authors note that standard leads/pretrend tests are not feasible because treated legislators have few periods (p.669), so they rely on robustness checks instead. Threats addressed: seniority/learning (log seniority, seniority FE, cohort-year FE), anticipation of own future termination and mean reversion (matched NY/TX controls with the same number of terms served, p.670 and fn 13). Heterogeneity predicted by theory (lifetime vs consecutive limits, professionalism, salary) is used as validation (p.671).
extraction.scope: Population: state legislators in 14 term-limited states (16 chambers), U.S., roughly 1991-2016, low-salience state legislative elections. Institution: term limits of three or more terms. Authors argue state legislatures resemble others on key attributes (Mooney 2009), so effects may generalize (p.663), but only 14 of 99 legislatures are covered (p.665). They explicitly disclaim normative conclusions about term limits as policy and aggregate legislative effort (p.674).

key_findings.finding: Termed-out (final-term) legislators have lower legislative productivity index, the main outcome. The effect is about one-quarter SD and is unchanged with chamber-party-year FE.
key_findings.numbers: Term limited = -0.24 (SE 0.03) in both columns; N=11,109; 4,642 legislators; outcome SD 1.00

key_findings.finding: Effect is robust to alternative counterfactuals. It shrinks with seniority controls but stays negative and significant. It is larger with matched NY/TX controls, which address both learning and anticipation.
key_findings.numbers: Log(seniority) -0.23 (SE 0.03); seniority FE -0.09 (0.03); cohort-year FE -0.09 (0.03); matched NY/TX -0.41 (0.03), N=11,416, 1,506 legislators

key_findings.finding: Floor attendance falls in the final term. Abstention rises from about 10% to 12.7% of votes, a proportional increase of about 27%. The authors say the effect is meaningfully larger than the term-length effect in Titiunik (2016).
key_findings.numbers: Percentage of floor votes = -2.70 (SE 0.53); -2.63 with party-year FE; outcome mean 90.48

key_findings.finding: Bill sponsorship falls in the final term, about 6% in proportional terms.
key_findings.numbers: Sponsored bills = -1.63 (SE 0.77) and -1.34 (SE 0.70) against mean 27.32; N=16,727; 6,207 legislators

key_findings.finding: Committee activity falls in the final term, about 8% in proportional terms.
key_findings.numbers: Committee activity = -0.31 (SE 0.06) and -0.30 (SE 0.05) against mean 3.84; N=16,255; 6,123 legislators

key_findings.finding: Heterogeneity fits theory. Effects are larger under lifetime limits than consecutive limits, in more professionalized legislatures, and where salaries are higher. Effects are also larger in California and Oklahoma, where limits are cumulative.

measures: Legislator productivity index: first PCA component of (log) bills sponsored, committee activity index, and percent of floor votes participated (p.666-667).

Committee activity index: 0 non-member, 1 member, 2 vice chair, 3 chair, summed over committees in a chamber-term; weights admitted to be somewhat arbitrary but results claimed not to depend on them (p.666).
Bills sponsored per legislator-term; data show mean 27 per year, SD 30 across legislators, within-legislator SD 17 (p.666).
Floor-vote participation: share of roll calls with a recorded yes or no vote (p.667). Some states record only final-passage votes (p.667).
Ideology: W-NOMINATE first dimension (negative = liberal, positive = conservative), absolute value as extremity (p.668). Party-split W-NOMINATE (Table 5).

Interest-group ratings: percent of votes aligned with a group's position, from Project Vote Smart or group sites, for abortion, business, education, environment, guns, taxes, labor unions, and other (p.672).

Treatment: TermLimited = final term before a binding term limit. Term-limit type (lifetime vs consecutive vs cumulative) and state professionalism/salary are heterogeneity moderators (Appendix Table A.3, p.671).
limitations: Parallel-trend and lead/pretrend diagnostics are not feasible given the small fixed number of periods for treated legislators (p.669).

Controls are less senior than the treated legislators; if productivity-seniority is concave, estimates overstate the effect (p.668-669). Log-seniority, seniority FE and cohort-year FE partly address this, but at a cost to functional-form assumptions (p.670).
Control legislators may anticipate their own future term limits, which would bias the comparison (p.670). Mean reversion may also contribute to the within-state estimate (fn 13, p.670).
Party control over committee assignments and bill coordination means effects may partly reflect party strategy rather than individual choice (p.666).
Half of the term-limited states cap bill introductions, though not stringently (p.666). Roll-call recording differs across states (p.667), though comparisons are within chamber-term.
Data collection is manual and labor-intensive (about 100 hours per state), limiting coverage to 14 of 99 legislatures (p.665).
Termed-out legislators may still face electoral incentives through other offices, which attenuates estimates (p.671).

W-NOMINATE is coarse and may miss issue-specific shifts. Interest-group ratings only detect systematic shifts, not heterogeneous individual deviations (p.674). Groups select bills for their own agendas (p.672).

The paper cannot say whether freed-up time goes to leisure or constituent service, or what happens to aggregate legislative effort (p.674). Mechanisms (voter attention, party, interest groups) are not identified (p.675).
Normative conclusions about term limits are explicitly disclaimed (p.674). Appendix content (Tables A.1, A.3; Figures A.3-A.4) is not in the extracted text and is unverified here.

short_quotes.quote: Elections appear to induce incumbents to allocate their effort toward observable measures of productivity

Abstract conclusion: elections shape effort even in low-salience settings but less so ideological positioning (fragment starts at rect edge).
Data allow fine-grained measures of how incumbents allocate effort.
Summary: termed-out legislators sponsor fewer bills, do less committee service, and attend fewer votes.
Multiple DiD designs give consistent evidence for the effects of electoral incentives.
Null ideology result fits a view where voters are poorly informed about candidate positions.
Elections in state legislatures are an important tool for shaping effort, against the view that low-salience elections leave legislators unconstrained (fragment).
Term-limit debate was well funded and has produced a deep academic literature.
Candidate moderation is weaker in state legislative elections than federal ones.
Consistent with voter inattention to state legislators' own behavior.
Threat of reelection can change officeholder actions even when outcomes do not depend on their ideology or effort.
Mechanisms of democracy seen in term-limited legislatures should generalize to other electoral contexts.
Low salience and low voter information make state legislatures a hard test of accountability models (fragment).
Prior designs (Besley and Case; List and Sturm) use within-state variation in lame-duck governors.
Lame-duck selection could produce an offsetting positive difference, biasing estimates down (fragment).
Alt, Bueno de Mesquita and Rose design assumes the type distribution of first-term governors is unchanged when the limit is extended.
Ferraz and Finan restrict the sample to barely-winning first-term mayors who win a second term.
Design requires non-staggered terms, so several state senates are excluded.
Hypothesis: incentives push legislators to observable effort to sway voter inferences.
Missing roll-call votes is one of the most basic forms of legislator shirking.
Legislators' webpages commonly list committee service and bills introduced, as advertising.
Committee effects should not be read as purely individual, since party assigns committees.
Bill sponsorship stats: mean 27 per legislator-year, SD 30 across legislators, 17 within.
Bill-level dataset records sponsor, name, summary, and whether the bill became law.
Over 16 million individual roll-call votes linked to specific candidates.
Cross-state differences in roll-call availability do not affect results because comparisons are within chamber and term.
Ideology is scaled with the W-NOMINATE algorithm.
W-NOMINATE sign convention: negative is more liberal, positive is more conservative.
Main estimate is a decrease of about one-quarter SD in the productivity index, across all three components.
Log-seniority specification keeps comparisons within legislatures but imposes a parametric form.
Anticipation concern: legislators who will be termed out may change effort in early terms.
New York and Texas chosen as non-term-limited control states, straightforward to digitize.
Committee activity index falls about 0.3 points from a mean of 3.8, roughly 8% proportionally.
Lifetime limits weaken incentives more, and the estimate is larger in those states, as expected.
Section heading: termed-out legislators do not seem to shift platforms.
First column outcome is the absolute value of W-NOMINATE.
Interest-group scores of issue-specific voting used to test ideological shifts.
Data reshaped so each row is a legislator ranked by interest group in a term.
Conclusion: electoral incentives influence how legislators allocate effort in important ways.
Elections induce effort toward observable productivity; once term-limited, legislators sponsor fewer bills and attend fewer votes.
Candidate moderation and election outcomes are muted in state legislatures.
Term-limit critique: final-term shirking by incumbents who no longer need reelection.
Caveat: freed-up time could go to leisure or to other constituent service, so shirking is not established.
Caution: findings are not a basis for the normative term-limit debate; they show how elections shape reelection-minded behavior.

summary_md:
Fouirnaies and Hall use term limits in 14 U.S. state legislatures (16 chambers, roughly 1991-2016) to ask whether reelection incentives change what legislators do. They compare each incumbent's binding final term with that same person's earlier terms, against same-chamber-year colleagues, using legislator and chamber-year fixed effects. In the final term, a PCA productivity index falls by 0.24 SD (N=11,109 legislator-terms). The drop ranges from -0.09 with seniority fixed effects to -0.41 with matched NY/TX controls. Roll-call participation falls 2.7 points from a mean of 90.5, bill sponsorship falls about 6% (-1.63 from a mean of 27.3 bills), and committee activity falls about 8%. Ideology does not move. |W-NOMINATE| changes by +0.02, the party-split estimates are about 0, and interest-group ratings across seven issue areas show no systematic shift. The authors read this as elections shaping visible effort, not positions. They add that legislators who leave to run for another office keep their electoral incentives, so the estimates are a lower bound.

For Paul's system, the paper matters in four places. (1) The receptivity layer cites it for a 0.60 "less responsive" multiplier on retiring members. The paper measured effort, not responsiveness to pressure. Its null on positions argues against reading the drop as movability, and its footnote 14 contradicts the retiring list, which includes members running for other office. (2) Several measures treat roll-call participation and sponsorship volume as dispositions or costly signals: diligence, the C criterion, the agenda volume and say-do path A. The paper shows these move with electoral status inside the same person. (3) The paper finds that effort and position separate cleanly, which supports keeping influence and alignment on separate axes. (4) Prospective test H2 cites this paper, but under it, retiring members' reduced activity can produce a correlation with no responsiveness behind it. The evidence comes from state legislatures with exogenous, binding limits. In Congress, retirement is voluntary and self-selected, so the effect transfers only weakly.

bearings.paper_claim: Removing reelection incentives lowers visible effort: the productivity index falls -0.24 SD (SE 0.03), with a range of -0.09 to -0.41 across specifications. Ideological positioning does not shift: |W-NOMINATE| +0.02 (SE 0.01), the party-split estimates are about 0, and interest-group ratings show no systematic change. The authors argue that legislators who run for other offices keep their electoral incentives, so the estimates are likely a lower bound.
bearings.paper_location: Tables 2-3 p.669-670; Table 5 p.673; Figure 2 p.674; main text and fn 14 p.672
bearings.system_side: incent_mult = 0.60 for every member on fec/retiring_members.txt. The docstring (receptivity_layer.py:15-16) cites Fouirnaies & Hall for final-term members reducing 'effort/responsiveness'; the retiring list header calls them 'less responsive to pressure'. The factor enters pressure_mult = clip(susc*incent*pt, 0.50, 1.60). The list header says it 'Includes members seeking OTHER office (Golden/Barr/Stefanik etc.)', and Andy Barr is the first entry. Line 129 (and docstring lines 17-19) also attribute the competitiveness term 1+.30(comp-0.5) to Fouirnaies-Hall, but the paper does not test seat competitiveness.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Weak for the 0.60 size and the 'responsiveness' reading. The paper estimates effort allocation in low-salience state chambers under exogenous, binding term limits. It does not estimate response to lobbying or money, and its null on positions points against extra movability or immovability. Congressional retirement is voluntary and self-selected, which is the confound the paper's within-person design is built to avoid. Its lower-bound argument (p.672) contradicts treating members who seek other office as having no electoral incentive. The direction (less effort in the final term) carries over; the magnitude and the mechanism of 'pressure response' do not.

Corrected: the lower-bound / other-office argument and fn 14 are on p.672, not p.671, and the argument is in the main text (fn 14 only cites Ban-Llaudet-Snyder on House runs). Line 129 attribution, line 227 pressure_mult clip, list header 'Includes members seeking OTHER office', Andy Barr first entry: all confirmed.

bearings.paper_claim: Floor-vote participation is state-dependent within the same legislator. It falls 2.70 points (SE 0.53) from a mean of 90.48 in the final term, about a 27% proportional rise in abstention. Committee activity falls about 8% (-0.31 from 3.84).
bearings.system_side: diligence_z is the mean of z-log votes_cast within chamber (with a full-term guard at 25% of the chamber median) and LEP follow-through. It is labelled a C-role disposition and enters susceptibility at -0.20. Members on the retiring list therefore get lower diligence and higher susc, which partly offsets their incent 0.60. Electoral status enters the pressure term twice, with opposite signs, and is never modelled explicitly.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Moderate. Missing votes is a universal congressional behaviour, and the paper's within-person identification is cleaner than anything the system has. However, the state final-term drop of about 3 points is small next to the cross-member spread in congressional votes_cast. It matters most for members in their final Congress, or those campaigning for another office, whose absences are campaign-driven. The disposition reading holds only after electoral status is held fixed.

bearings.paper_claim: In the final term, effort falls (sponsorship -6%, committee activity -8%, participation -2.7 points) while positions stay flat (W-NOMINATE and interest-group nulls).
bearings.system_side: Under the protocol, H2 (labelled Byrne/F&H) tests Spearman(frozen pressure_mult, |overall-tier movement|) after the freeze. pressure_mult carries the 0.60 retiring factor. Tier movement depends on new evidence events, and retiring members produce fewer of them under this paper's effect, so a positive H2 could arise mechanically from lower activity rather than from responsiveness. The paper also predicts no true position change from the F&H channel.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Moderate as a threat to interpretation. It applies only if tier movement is driven by evidence volume. If the contract is still unfrozen, a reported retiring/other-office stratum could be added. If it is frozen, any H2 result should carry this caveat. This is analysis, not a look, and stays UNVERIFIED until reproduced (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Bill sponsorship volume falls about 6% when reelection incentives end (-1.63, SE 0.77, mean 27.32; N=16,727) with no ideological change. Sponsorship volume partly reflects electoral advertising (legislators' webpages list bills introduced) rather than position.
bearings.paper_location: Table 4 cols 3-4 p.671; p.666; Table 5 p.673
bearings.system_side: Agenda sums signed row contribution times |topic weight| over all selected rows (no per-member volume normalization), and Leg% blends agenda with an efficiency component before percent-ranking. A member's final-Congress drop in activity therefore lowers the agenda component of Leg% with no change in stance. Stance enters as the sign of each contribution, so volume and direction stay distinguishable, which fits the paper's finding that effort and position separate.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Weak. The 6% effect at the state level is small, and in Congress it would touch only members in their final Congress or those running for other office. The paper supports the influence-vs-alignment split. It does not address the 4:2:1 role weights or cosponsorship.

Code corrected: live_legislative_pillar.py:47-57 sums signed row contribution times |topic weight| into agenda; lines 21-26 are the percentrank helper. Agenda is one side of an agenda/efficiency blend, so a final-Congress activity drop lowers the agenda component of Leg%, not Leg% one-for-one. Stance enters as the sign of each contribution, not as a separate multiplier.

bearings.paper_claim: Sponsorship is effort directed at voters' inferences, not a revelation of position: it falls when reelection ends while ideology stays flat. Legislators advertise bills introduced on their webpages.
bearings.paper_location: p.666 (advertising, observable-effort hypothesis); Table 4 p.671; Table 5 p.673
bearings.system_side: Path A treats an authored or original-cosponsored bill in the category as the costly signal that corroborates Champion or Defender. The overall gate's thin_high_volume rule (at least 10 direct bills with no more than 20% advanced) treats high-volume introduction as cheap talk.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Weak. The paper supports the thin_high_volume reading, since introduction volume responds to electoral display. extraction.title: Political Advertising after Citizens United: IPTW-FE for MSMs
extraction.venue: Metadata hint said "Working paper". The text is a manuscript dated February 9, 2026 with "Comments welcome"; no venue, journal or series is stated.
extraction.coverage: Read the entire extracted text file (3,671 lines, 123,945 bytes; the 104,593-char hint was wrong) in four chunks: front matter, Sections 1-7, references, and Appendices A-D including all figure captions and numeric residue. Read all 90 highlights in the single annotation file (559bf8cc8dc4.json). Paul's markup: 90 Highlight annotations, all by Paul Goff, all with empty content, no sticky notes, no dates, and three highlight colours (yellow, green, pink). Covered text is paraphrased, not reproduced, under the copyright rule. Scope check: the paper contains no lobbying-network, path-finding, allocation, or legislator-level content; its only network-adjacent material is the interest-group ad treatment and the cited literature.
extraction.research_question: Do independent interest-group TV ads affect Senate and gubernatorial vote shares and turnout after Citizens United, and can an MSM estimator be adjusted for time-constant unmeasured confounding (unit-level heterogeneity) when only a single outcome is observed?
extraction.theory: Time-varying treatment with feedback: campaigns and groups respond to each other's ad decisions, so treatment and covariates co-evolve, causing time-varying confounding. Sequential ignorability is a poor fit when groups target markets with persuadable voters by a metric the researcher does not observe (p.3, p.8). The paper proposes a unit-specific sequential ignorability (Assumption 1, p.11): conditional on an unmeasured time-constant alpha_i, treatment is independent of future potential outcomes and covariates. The MSM is a g-computation-style marginal model for treatment histories (pp.8-9, 15).
extraction.data: Unit: media market by race (market-race), weekly panel over the campaign window from primary to general election (8 to 40 weeks, median 20; p.25). Races: US Senate and gubernatorial general elections, 2010-2020 (pp.6, 25). Sample after dropping no-treatment-variation races: N = 467 market-races for Democratic IG ads and N = 623 for Republican IG ads (p.25). Sources: Wesleyan Media Project ad data covering all broadcast stations (Fowler et al., 2019); CQ Voting and Elections Collection outcomes; CVAP from US Census; RealClearPolitics polls; county-to-media-market mapping from Sides et al. (2022) (p.6). Simulations (Section 5, p.21): n in {200, 500, 1000, 3000} units, rho = n/T in {5, 10, 50}, 500 Monte Carlo replications (p.23).
extraction.method: Proposed IPTW-FE: a two-step procedure. Step 1 fits a parametric logit propensity model with unit-specific fixed effects alpha_i by conditional MLE (incidental-parameters setting). Step 2 builds stabilized inverse-probability weights over the last k+1 periods and solves the weighted MSM estimating equation (weighted least squares for the identity link) (pp.15-17). Theorem 1 gives sqrt(N)-consistency and asymptotic normality with a sandwich variance, with N and T growing at the same rate (p.17); appendix proofs in Appendix A (pp.41-53). Comparators: IPTW with no fixed effects (race-level FE only), and a naive approach that ignores time-varying covariates. Empirical MSM (p.26): E[Y_i(d) | R_i] = gamma_R + gamma_1 * sum_{k=0}^{4} d_{T-k}, race-specific intercepts, effect of one extra week of IG ads in the last five weeks. Weighting model covariates (p.27): lagged Dem poll share and square, undecided/third-party share, Republican negativity over six weeks, cumulative ads by each party and squares, market-race FE. Simulations report bias, SE and 90% CI coverage (pp.22-24).
extraction.identification: Unit-specific sequential ignorability (Assumption 1, p.11): conditional on the past treatment history, the covariate history and an unmeasured time-constant alpha_i, treatment is independent of future potential outcomes and future covariates. This allows time-constant measured and unmeasured confounding plus time-varying measured confounding, but rules out time-varying unmeasured confounding (p.12). Positivity is needed. Within-unit treatment switching is required (p.1). A no-anticipation assumption is built into the covariate process (p.11). Truncated MSMs (fixed k lags) are used so the number of propensity parameters, and hence incidental-parameter bias, stays limited (pp.10-11). Identification is not from a pre-period or a difference-in-differences design, because there is one endpoint outcome per unit (p.5, p.4).
extraction.scope: Population: US Senate and gubernatorial general-election market-races, 2010-2020, using broadcast TV ads by independent interest groups (ads by candidates and parties are excluded; p.6). Unit of analysis is the media market (not county or state). Era: pre- and post-Citizens United (2010 decision), with a split at Trump's candidacy. Methodological scope: truncated MSMs with a fixed-length treatment history and a fixed-length parameter vector, with N and T growing at the same rate (pp.10, 15). Empirical findings are about down-ballot races and are not generalised to presidential races.

key_findings.finding: The effectiveness of Democratic IG ads is concentrated in the post-Trump era (after 2016 per Abstract and p.5; text on p.30 says 2015). Democratic ads more effective at increasing Democratic votes and reducing Republican votes; differences significant at alpha = 0.1.

key_findings.numbers: Imputed propensity scores 0.01 and 0.99 (p.19); no-variation races dropped in main results.

limitations: Assumption 1 is violated by time-varying unmeasured confounding, a limitation the paper shares with linear fixed effects and difference-in-differences (p.12).
With one endpoint outcome per unit, a doubly robust estimator with outcome-regression models is not feasible without strong assumptions (p.19).
Truncated MSMs rule out cumulative full-treatment-history terms; long-term effects cannot be estimated while adjusting for unmeasured confounding (p.11).
Consistency requires a correctly specified parametric propensity model for covariates, plus fixed-length parameter vectors (pp.14-15). The model-specific results are asymptotic.
Finite-sample second-order bias scales with propensity extremity and short T; strong heterogeneity is worse. A jackknife correction is left to future work (pp.18-19).
Positivity: fixed effects are not identified for units never or always treated; the three remedies (omit, impute, bound alpha) each trade bias for variance (pp.19-20).
Residual unmeasured confounding remains a worry the authors acknowledge (p.32), though placebo tests are null (p.33).
The paper assumes no interference across media markets (p.6) and treats ads as weeks of presence, not ad counts; the comparison with Sides et al. is therefore indirect (p.32).
Only broadcast television ads are measured; the approach uses the market-race as the unit, and county outcomes are mapped to markets (p.6).

Simulation evidence uses 500 MC replications and only the correctly specified MSM in the main text; the proposed estimator is slightly biased under high heterogeneity even with the true propensity score (p.24).
Internal inconsistency: the Trump-candidacy split is dated 2015 on p.30 but 2016 in the Abstract (p.1), p.5 and the Figure 4 caption (p.29).
Metadata inconsistency to note: the text does not state a venue; the title and authors match the hint.
measures: Outcomes (p.6): Democratic share of the two-party vote (CQ returns); Democratic turnout % (Dem votes / CVAP); Republican turnout % (Rep votes / CVAP); placebo outcomes: lagged two-party vote, lagged Dem and Rep turnout from the previous election for the same office, and pre-election Democratic poll share.

Treatment (p.6): binary D_it = 1 if an independent group (any interest or advocacy group other than candidate or party, including dark-money groups and PACs) ran TV ads in market i in week t; separate analyses for Democratic and Republican groups; cumulative weeks in last five weeks of campaign.

Covariates (p.27): average Democratic poll share in previous week and its square; average undecided or third-party share; Republican negativity (attack ads) over last six weeks; cumulative ads shown by Democrat and Republican and squares; attack-ad coding from Wesleyan data (p.6).
Simulation measures (pp.22-23): bias, standard error (HC2 sandwich), and 90% CI coverage for tau_F and tau_C.

summary_md:
Blackwell and Yamauchi (manuscript, 9 Feb 2026) ask whether TV ads run by independent interest groups after Citizens United changed vote shares and turnout. The sample is US Senate and gubernatorial general elections, 2010-2020, measured as weekly media-market by race panels (N = 467 market-races for Democratic-group ads, 623 for Republican). The methods problem is feedback: ads and campaign conditions shape each other, and groups may target persuadable markets on information the researcher cannot see. The authors fit a propensity model with a fixed effect for each unit (estimated by conditional MLE) and use it to build inverse-probability weights for a truncated marginal structural model. They prove root-N consistency when N and T grow together. In simulations (500 replications) the estimator beats IPTW without fixed effects, although some bias remains when heterogeneity is high.

Empirically, Democratic-group ads raise the Democratic two-party share, mostly by raising Democratic turnout, and the effect is concentrated after Trump's candidacy. Republican-group ads show no effect. Placebo tests on lagged outcomes come out near zero. Effects are significant only at alpha 0.1, the text gives no point estimates, and the Trump split is dated 2015 on p.30 but 2016 elsewhere.

For Paul's systems this is mainly a methods paper. It sharpens the caution on Mentat's fixed-effects regressions of sector growth on spending, and it shows a placebo-outcome check that the prospective receptivity contract lacks. It also gives one weak, party-asymmetric data point on Terrier's split between persuasion and mobilization. It says nothing about legislators, so it cannot support the competitiveness multiplier or any part of the flip model's money terms.

bearings.paper_claim: Unit fixed-effects regressions are biased when treatment and time-varying covariates feed back on each other (citing Imai & Kim 2019 and Sobel 2012). The paper's remedy moves the fixed effects into a propensity model and requires a binary treatment that switches within units, a correctly specified parametric propensity model, and N and T growing together. Simulations use n of 200-3000 with T of at least 4; in the empirical panel, campaign windows run 8-40 weeks.
bearings.system_side: OLS of sector-year spending DVs (contributions_real_m; LobbyView lobbying for the L*-LV tests) on a growth term with sector FE plus controls (pres_year, midterm_year, exp_dem_house, exp_dem_senate), with year-FE variants (variant year_fe) and first-differences-with-year-effects (FDY) checks; inference is a wild cluster restricted bootstrap by sector, DESCRIPTIVE when only 2 sectors. Reference values in the Codex review file sgs_review.R: L3-LV coefficient +0.352 (n=77) becomes -0.477 with year FE, and the FDY coefficient is -0.537 over 71 adjacent pairs (window and sample as set in that test's spec).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only the diagnosis transfers, not the estimator. Applies to any sector-year panel where lobbying or giving is the outcome of a growth regressor that may itself respond to past spending.

summary_issues: 'Effects are significant only at alpha 0.1' overstates the text: alpha 0.1 is stated only for the pre/post-Trump era DIFFERENCES (p.30, line ~1209). For the main Figure 3 effects the text says only that methods 'generally agree on the direction and significance', with no level given.

Bearing 1 system description (in rel, echoed by 'fixed-effects regressions of sector growth on spending') is reversed in direction: spending is the DV and growth the regressor; also log DVs, tossup/trend controls and a lagged/AR lobbying term were not found in the cited code, and the sign-flip values come from sgs_review.R reference values, not a brain record.
Gap item on Mentat's transfer graph (89% oppose IE split) was not verified here; treat as UNVERIFIED.
gaps_exposed: No component estimates a causal effect of money, ads or lobbying. Every money-response constant in the influence engine (WM/WP, HALFF, MAXSHIFT, COMPET_MULT amplitude and scale) is judgment. The paper shows the kind of design (weekly treatment panel, propensity weighting with unit fixed effects, placebo outcomes) that estimating them would need.
The prospective receptivity contract (H1/H2) has no negative-control or placebo look on pre-freeze outcomes, so it cannot tell responsiveness apart from a stable member trait.

The sector-growth regressions have no design that addresses feedback between lagged lobbying or giving and later covariates. The sign flips under year FE are reported but cannot be interpreted causally.

Neither Mentat nor Melange measures voter-facing outside spending as a treatment with timing. Mentat's transfer graph splits independent-expenditure dollars into support and oppose (89% oppose) but carries no week-level timing or outcome link.
Terrier's persuasion/mobilization weight wp is symmetric and fixed. No evidence base, including this paper, sets it by party or era.
flags: Voter-level evidence only. It must not be quoted as support for the competitiveness multiplier's reciprocity or for any legislator money response; reciprocity is NOT validated (D-104..D-108).

Pooled versus stratified: the Democratic-ad effect is concentrated after Trump's candidacy. Quote the pooled Democratic effect only with the era strata, or label it UNSTRATIFIED. Window: Senate and gubernatorial races 2010-2020; denominators N = 467 (Democratic-group ads) and 623 (Republican-group ads) market-races.
Internal inconsistency: the Trump-era split is dated 2015 on p.30 but 2016 in the Abstract, on p.5 and in the Figure 4 caption.
Results are significant only at alpha 0.1, and the text gives no point estimates (figures only). Do not invent magnitudes.
Any IPTW-FE-style re-analysis of Paul's data by an agent stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
The paper does not argue for either rejected SNA proposal, and it does not use LDA.
paul_alignment: Paul records no takeaways. Both bibliography entries (folder Causal & Methodological, and a5b9f5a95891) are bare citations, which fits his component note that the Causal & Methodological folder is unannotated. His 90 highlights fall almost entirely on method: fixed effects inside the propensity score, the single-outcome setting, the need for treatment switching, the positivity remedies (drop, bound or impute alpha), the simulation design, and three pink conclusion highlights. That suggests he values the paper as an estimation template, not for its findings about ads. The bearings above agree with that reading. The paper's contribution is the confounding diagnosis and the placebo practice, both of which the system's validation discipline could absorb. No note of his is stale relative to the system, because none links this paper to a component.

related.why: Both papers question unit and two-way fixed-effects designs under feedback. Blackwell & Yamauchi cite the 2019 Imai & Kim paper on the same problem. Together they underwrite reading the sector-growth year-FE sign flip as non-causal.
Weimer uses Monte Carlo as a negative control. Blackwell & Yamauchi use placebo outcomes from before treatment. Both are falsification checks that the prospective contract lacks.

Both papers bear on campaign persuasion and its returns, and Broockman co-authored the Hewitt et al. (2024) experiments used here as a magnitude benchmark (1.2-2.3 pp). Together they inform Terrier's split between persuasion and mobilization.

Kalla's experiment identifies the effect of money on legislators' access. This paper identifies the effect of outside spending on voters. The flip model's money assumptions need evidence of the first kind, which this paper does not supply.

extraction.document_type: Working paper (SSRN), update to the book Congress: A Political-Economic History of Roll Call Voting (Poole and Rosenthal, 1997)
extraction.coverage: Whole text read: all 1,743 lines of the extracted text (46,871 chars), in one pass. Annotation JSON read in full: 57 Paul Goff markup items (56 highlights and 1 FreeText). Colors: 48 yellow, 7 green (p.2, p.17, p.19, p.20 x4), 1 pink (p.17). Lobbying, networks, path-finding, allocation, persuasion/turnout and text measurement are not addressed. Covered text in paul_markup is paraphrased, not quoted (copyright rule). Only one short quote is given (copyright rule).
extraction.research_question: Have the trends identified in Congress (1997) toward polarization and one-dimensionality in roll call voting continued through the 105th Congress, and does the 1994 Republican takeover represent a sharp break? Secondary: do DW-NOMINATE and alternative scaling methods recover essentially the same legislator positions, and how does the U.S. Congress fit the spatial model compared with other legislatures? (Abstract p.2; Sec. 1 p.3.)
extraction.theory: Basic spatial theory of ideology (Ordeshook 1976; Hinich and Pollard 1981; Enelow and Hinich 1984; Hinich and Munger 1994): legislators have ideal points in a low-dimensional policy space and choose the outcome closer to them. Dynamic extension: legislator coordinates are polynomial functions of time (Appendix eq. A1, p.19). Roll call utility is a normal-error probit over a Gaussian-type distance with dimension salience weights (eqs. A2-A4, p.20).
extraction.data: U.S. House and Senate roll calls, Congresses 1-105 (1789-1998). Unit: legislator-roll call choice (Yea or Nay; abstentions discarded, endnote 9, p.30). Legislators included if they cast at least 25 votes in at least one Congress (endnote 1, p.30). House: 38,740 scalable roll calls, 10,208 scalable representatives, 10,495,639 choices (Table 1, p.23). Senate: 41,165 roll calls, 1,794 senators, 2,697,691 choices (Table 1, p.24). Joint House-Senate scaling: 79,905 roll calls, 11,389 unique legislators, 13,193,330 choices, with 613 members serving in both chambers as "glue" (Table 3, p.27; p.10). Presidents Eisenhower through Clinton included as members of both chambers using CQ presidential support roll calls (p.10). Comparison sets (Table 4, p.28-29): 105th House (946 roll calls, 443 legislators), 105th Senate (486, 101), Third and Fourth European Parliament, 1841 British Parliament, French National Assembly 1951-56, Czech Parliament 1993-97, 1995 Polish Parliament, UN General Assembly sets.
extraction.method: DW-NOMINATE (dynamic, weighted, nominal three-step estimation): normal (probit) errors replacing D-NOMINATE's logit errors; per-dimension salience weights w_k; legislator coordinates polynomial in time, estimated as constant (v=0) and linear (v=1) only (p.5-6, Appendix p.19-20). Estimated by maximum likelihood over the joint choice likelihood (eq. A4, p.20). Comparators: Poole's non-parametric optimal classification (rank ordering that maximizes correct classification; one dimension only; Poole 1997, 2000), Heckman-Snyder factor analysis (p.9). Fit measured by percent correctly classified, APRE, and geometric mean probability (Table 1 notes, p.24-25). Party polarization measured by mean within- and between-party pairwise distances (Figs 7-8, p.14) and percent party overlap (Fig 9, p.15). Joint scaling of both chambers estimated with optimal classification (Table 3, p.27).
extraction.identification: Not a causal design; this is measurement of ideal points. Ideal points are identified by maximum likelihood across roll calls with the salience weight for dimension 1 set to one and the probit error variance normalized to 1 (p.8). Linear trends are estimated for legislators serving at least 3 (or 5) Congresses; the authors concede the 3-Congress threshold lets random walkers appear linear, which biases toward the polynomial models (p.6). Joint House-Senate scaling assumes the 613 glue members hold fixed positions across chambers (p.10); the authors call this "reasonably supported" from the classification drop of about 1 point (p.11-12).
extraction.scope: Population: all roll call votes and members of the U.S. House and Senate, 1789-1998 (Congresses 1-105). Substantive focus: Post-Reconstruction Democrat/Republican party system, 1879-1998, with extra attention to recent Congresses (p.12). Cross-national comparison (Sec. 6, p.16-17): a few legislatures at single time spans. Institution: the U.S. Congress plus selected parliaments. Era: Post-Reconstruction and modern polarization (1879-1998).

summary_md:
Poole and Rosenthal update their 1997 roll-call study through the 105th Congress (1789-1998) using DW-NOMINATE, a dynamic probit spatial model of legislator ideal points. Four results matter here. First, legislator positions are close to fixed over a career: the linear time-trend model adds only about 0.3 points of classification over the constant model (House 85.65 to 85.96; Senate 84.04 to 84.40). Second, Congress has become one-dimensional: the second dimension now adds under 1 percent. Third, party overlap on dimension 1 is near zero: under 1.5% in both chambers over the last five Congresses, and none in the last three Senates. Fourth, polarization rose smoothly, with no break at 1994. A non-parametric rank method produces nearly the same orders (Spearman .960 House, .981 Senate). The donor and primary claim that Paul highlighted in pink rests on a cited working paper that this text does not present.

For the system as built, the paper is a measurement baseline. It is not an engine input. DW-NOMINATE appears only as a control (fec/members/dw_control.py) and through per-Congress Nokken-Poole scores used as a criterion. The sharpest consequence is for the say-do gate's Path V. One CU-aligned final-passage vote counts as corroboration, and in a polarized, one-dimensional chamber that vote mostly records the member's party. A read-only check confirms strong party sorting in several categories (details in bearings). That check is UNVERIFIED. The paper also explains why drift-based susceptibility criteria have little true variance to detect. It argues for using an ideal-point control rather than a bare party dummy wherever party-confounded tiers are interpreted, as in the CFPB isolation. The paper does nothing for lobbying, money effects, pathfinding or allocation.

related.why: Aref and Neal partition signed House co-sponsorship networks (1981-2017) and find the optimal 2-partition and especially the 3-partition leave fewer frustrated edges than the party partition, with a fluid third coalition. NOMINATE dim1 is a natural benchmark for whether those members are more than near-center moderates.
Earlier optimal signed partition of House and Senate co-sponsorship networks (sessions 96-114); its coalitions can be checked against DW-NOMINATE ideal points.
Bonica estimates candidate and contributor ideal points from contribution records and compares them with DW-NOMINATE; relevant to the donors-and-primaries claim this paper leaves unevidenced.
A formal model (no data) of how presidential going-public can raise legislative polarization; a mechanism for the polarization trend this paper measures.

backlinks.why: D-NOMINATE gives the low-dimensional account of elite roll-call ideology. This paper argues mass opinion is multidimensional relative to the elite axis, which is why elite-middle moves do not map onto a single median voter.

Fouirnaies & Hall's ideology null rests on W-NOMINATE scaling of state roll calls, from the NOMINATE family Poole reviews. The paper itself states the scaling may be too coarse to detect issue-specific shifts (p.668, p.673).

Jacoby cites Poole and Rosenthal [19] for spatial models and Voteview [16] for the alpha rates (Table 2). This vault item (D-NOMINATE after 10 years) is not itself cited; the centrist-band reversal plausibly depends on that kind of ideal-point scale, though the paper does not name the scale it used.
Verified item. Porter benchmarks its SVD against Poole-Rosenthal Optimal Classification (Polit. Anal. 2000), not DW-NOMINATE. The link is a same-family scaling comparison, not the same method.
Both use roll-call matrices: NOMINATE scales ideology and Ringe and Wilson extract leadership centrality from binary votes. Melange rejected DW-NOMINATE vote edges (brain vote-edges section).
